title: stochastic-routing-hypothesis-diary
body:
Context / why I wrote this
- Follow-up scratchpad from the 2026-03-09 narrow outage where ~3% of production requests (mostly long-context chat) experienced unexpected fallbacks to the small-capacity 'cheap' pool.
- Symptoms were intermittent: not correlated to a single AZ, showed up across us-east-1a and us-east-1c, lasted ~7m in bursts, then quiet.
- Primary suspicion: stochastic tie-breaking in the smart-router combined with stale capacity view (KV cache TTL mismatch).

Quick summary of previous notes (condensed)
- Timeline: 03:11 UTC first spike, 03:18 UTC larger spike, 03:25 services auto-recovered after cache invalidation TTL expired (~10s).
- Alerts fired: route-fallback-rate > 2% for production-route/*, SLO noise for token-latency, multiple 503->fallback traces seen in traces.
- Operators applied manual rollout to pin routing policy (policy-id=policy_chat_prod_v3) which suppressed further spikes, suggesting policy selection is involved.

Commands I ran (local dev/probe commands)
- reproduce probe (from devbox):
  curl -v -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TESTKEY' \
    -d '{"model":"chat-3b","input":"hello","max_tokens":200}' \
    https://proxy-stub.internal.redwood/api/v1/generate | jq .
  -> sometimes returns 200 from primary pool, sometimes returns 202 FALLBACK:route=cheap-pool\\n
- check router state (kvs):
  redis-cli -h router-kv-01 GET route:chat-3b:policy
  => '{\"policy_id\":\"policy_chat_prod_v3\", \"stamp\":1670000000}'
  redis-cli -h router-kv-01 TTL route:chat-3b:policy
  => -1 (no TTL)  <-- suspicious

- service health endpoints:
  curl http://pool-primary-1:8080/health | jq .
  => {"ok":true,"inflight":256,"capacity_tokens":860000}  (normal)
  curl http://pool-cheap-1:8080/health | jq .
  => {"ok":true,"inflight":24,"capacity_tokens":60000}  (normal)

- dump of router decision logs (sample)
  [2026-03-09T03:18:12.345Z] route=chat-3b req_id=aa11 severity=INFO action=select_candidate candidates=[primary,cheap] scores=[0.921,0.908] pick=cheap reason=stochastic-tiebreak rand=0.981
  [2026-03-09T03:18:12.346Z] route=chat-3b req_id=aa11 action=fallback to=cheap cause=policy-fallback-limit

Error / log snippets seen in production traces
- proxy logs: "policy-selection: policy mismatch between kv and in-memory config (route=chat-3b)" (intermittent)
- proxy stack: "panic: out_of_bounds access in routeIndex" (rare, recovered) --> correlates with a single host restart window
- tracing snippet (jaeger): span shows candidate selection -> decision node: 'stochastic_tiebreak' -> fallback=true -> fallback_reason: 'policy-compatibility'

Hypotheses (ordered by likelihood)
1) Stochastic tie-breaker bias + high request burst + lack of strong TTL on routing policy KV: the router caches an older policy with no TTL (redis returned -1) and the decision function ends up in a narrow margin where random draws push to cheap pool more often. The 'no TTL' came from a rollout that wrote policy without timestamp/ttl.
2) Race between policy hot-reload and candidate scoring: config reloads (policy update) happen in the control plane; some nodes get new policy but still have an old ephemeral scoring function or delayed kernel; if scoring thresholds change slightly, near-threshold requests diverge deterministically.
3) Health transient + probing: one primary host briefly returned an inflated inflight count (instrument hiccup), router penalizes primary and shifts requests. This is plausible but health endpoints looked fine for most hosts.
4) A bug in the stochastic tiebreak implementation that amplifies randomness when scores are very close — e.g., an unbounded RNG seed per-node that correlated with request patterns and time-of-day.

Notes from small experiments
- Forcing TTL on the policy key to 15s reduced the occurrence in dev-probe.
  redis-cli -h router-kv-01 SETEX route:chat-3b:policy 15 '{"policy_id":"policy_chat_prod_v3","stamp":1670000001}'
  -> reproduced fewer fallbacks over 2000 probes.
- Turning off stochastic tie-break (deterministic max-score pick) eliminated the fallback spike in our local replay of the 03:18 window.
- Simulating burst load with siege against proxy shows fallback rate increases non-linearly around 1200 rps sustained for >10s.

Immediate mitigations (what we did during incident)
- pin policy at control-plane (force voters to policy_chat_prod_v3) for 30m window.
- short TTL sweep: pushed TTL 10s for all route:* keys to avoid stale keys without explicit eviction.
- rolled routing-proxy on 4 hosts where panics were seen (rolling restart).

Follow-ups / things to do (action items)
- [P1] Add TTL enforcement on all route policy writes in control-plane. If a policy is intentionally infinite, write explicit 'infinite' flag, don't leave null TTL. (owner: Marco)
- [P1] Add canary-mode for stochastic_tiebreak: percentage rollouts and telemetry flag to dump random seeds and decision entropy metric (owner: Aisha).
- [P2] Instrument per-request policy version (policy_id & stamp) into tracing spans to quickly correlate mismatches. (owner: Claire)
- [P2] Add deterministic fallback override: if scores within delta < 0.005, prefer pool with active hot cache (kv cache hit metric). This reduces cold-hot oscillations. (owner: Omar)
- [P3] Postmortem write-up: include traffic profiles, sample traces, repro script, and tests to simulate near-threshold stochastic bias. (owner: Aisha)

Open questions (things I couldn't confirm yet)
- Why did the policy key have no TTL? Was it an intentional write by control-plane that omitted TTL, or a bug in the migration that removed TTLs? Need to grep control-plane writes.
- Are there correlated CloudWatch autoscaling events or host-level CPU/IOThrottling at the exact times? I didn't see any high CPU, but need deeper host metrics (kernel scheduler stalls?).
- Any correlation with the dedicated/different region routing table rollouts? We saw a spike across two AZs, could be control-plane multicast timing.

Repro script / steps (mini)
1) on dev cluster, seed router-kv with policy without TTL:
   redis-cli -h router-kv-01 SET route:chat-3b:policy '{"policy_id":"policy_chat_prod_v3","stamp":1670000000}'
2) start many concurrent probes (~1.2k rps) to /api/v1/generate via proxy-stub for 60s in bursts.
3) gather proxy logs with grep 'stochastic-tiebreak' and tally fallbacks.
4) repeat with SETEX TTL 15 and with deterministic tie-break to compare.

Notes to pass on to infra / control-plane
- Add validation to control-plane API: if policy write omits TTL, require explicit 'infinite' boolean or reject. That will prevent accidental no-TTL writes.
- Consider a short-term safety guard in router: if redis TTL == -1 treat as transient and fetch fresh config from control-plane endpoint (with small penalty) rather than silently accepting it.

Random scratch hypotheses (for later)
- RNG seeding correlated with monotonic timestamp on some hosts caused bursts of 'pick cheap' for buckets of requests — look at RNG implementation.
- If KV network latency spikes to redis replica, a node might see >100ms stale reads and assume older policy; need to measure redis read p50/p99 during incident.
- GC pause in Go runtime on a proxy node caused decision thread to retry and pick fallback. GC traces? enable GODEBUG gctrace for 24h in canary cluster.

Stuff I want to save in the postmortem
- decision log samples (sanitized request ids), redis responses (policy+ttl), host health snapshots, jaeger traces for 30 sample fallbacks, and the repro script.

Slack threads / people to ping
- #infra-controlplane (Marco)
- #serving-runtime (Claire, Omar)
- @ops-oncall for next incident (note: escalate earlier if fallback rate > 1.5% and sustained for 5m)

Final quick note to self
- This one feels like a small systems mismatch (policy TTL + stochastic tie-break). Easy to fix but sneaky in production because it only shows up on near-threshold scoring. Put extra tests around threshold boundaries.

--- end of scratchpad (will formalize into postmortem)
